c.tagline: Alagoas capital of turquoise natural pools, jangadas and 'Caribbean' beaches.

taxi.fareNote: City taxis are metered; ride-hailing apps like Uber and 99 are usually cheaper than street taxis.

emergency.note: 190 reaches the military police, 192 summons a SAMU ambulance, and 193 reaches the fire brigade.

hood_landmark.Cruz das Almas: Praia de Cruz das Almas, Maceió

avoid.reason: Caution outside the main beach strip (Pajuçara/Ponta Verde) at night

hood_desc: Maceió's iconic tourist beachfront, lined with high-rise hotels and a coconut-palm promenade, and the launch point for jangada raft trips out to the offshore natural pools; the classic first-timer base.
A lively upscale beach neighborhood between Pajuçara and Jatiúca with calm reef-protected water, a busy boardwalk, restaurants and bars; central, walkable and popular with visitors.
A trendy beachfront district with some of the city's best restaurants, beach bars and nightlife, plus surfable waves at its northern end; suits travelers wanting dining and going out.
A more local beach neighborhood north of the tourist core with a long strand, beach kiosks and a relaxed residential feel; good for a quieter, cheaper stay near the sand.
A tranquil northern coastal area of low-key beaches backed by coconut groves and eco-lodges, several kilometers from the busy tourist strip; suits travelers wanting quiet and nature over nightlife.

water.note: Drink bottled or filtered water; locals do not drink from the tap.

transit.hours: Buses run roughly 5am to midnight; a single light-rail (VLT) line runs limited daytime services, so late-night travel relies on taxis and ride-hailing apps.
transit.note: Maceió gets around mainly on its municipal and metropolitan bus network; a single diesel light-rail line (VLT / Maceió Urban Rail, run by CBTU) links the center with northern suburbs but is little used by tourists, who rely on buses, taxis and ride-hailing apps along the beach strip.
transit.pay: Pay cash to the driver or tap a rechargeable transit card on buses; a single bus fare is about R$4.50.

food.name: Sururu ao coco
food.desc: Tiny lagoon mussels raked from Lagoa Mundau and stewed in coconut milk with coriander and dende, served with rice or as a peppery caldo.

places.name: Barracas do Pontal da Barra
places.note: Lagoon-side shacks that shell the sururu the same morning; the source locals swear by.

places.name: Sururu de Capote
places.note: Beachfront restaurant built around the dish, from caldo to sururu risotto.

places.name: Peixarao
places.note: Generous seafood house known for its moqueca alagoana and sururu.

food.name: Peixada alagoana
food.desc: Firm reef fish poached in coconut milk with tomato, coriander, peppers and egg, thickened with pirao and shared straight from the pot.

places.name: Peixarao
places.note: Big portions of peixada and moqueca; a local standard for decades.

places.name: Lopana

places.name: Casa de Mainha
places.note: Home-style northeastern cooking near the craft pavilion, easy on the wallet.

food.name: Arroz de polvo
food.desc: Octopus simmered until tender then folded through rice cooked in its own stock with coconut milk and coriander; an Alagoan Sunday plate.

places.name: Wanchako

places.name: Lopana
places.note: Seafood rice dishes served family-style overlooking the beach.

places.name: Barracas do Pontal da Barra

food.desc: Sun-cured beef grilled and sliced over boiled or fried cassava with butter, curd cheese and vinaigrette; the sertao's contribution to the coast.

places.name: Casa de Mainha

food.name: Bolo de rolo and cocada
food.desc: Paper-thin sponge rolled around guava paste, sold next to trays of chewy coconut cocada and doce de leite; the region's sweet counter in one stall.

places.name: Mercado do Artesanato

places.name: Mercado da Producao

places.name: Orla da Pajucara vendors

food.desc: Juices pressed from northeastern fruit you rarely see elsewhere, tart mangaba and caja through to deep-red siriguela, served with ice or milk.

places.name: Orla da Pajucara kiosks

places.name: Casa de Mainha

landmarks: Pajuçara Natural Pools (Piscinas Naturais de Pajuçara)
Colorful jangada sailboats ferry bathers two kilometers offshore to crystal-clear reef pools teeming with fish, Maceió's signature low-tide experience.
Praia de Ponta Verde
The city's postcard urban beach curves palm-lined and calm around a reef-sheltered bay, with a lively promenade of coconut kiosks and beach clubs.
Pontal da Barra and Mundaú Lagoon
This lagoon-side fishing quarter is the cradle of filé lace embroidery, where artisan shops meet sunset boat tours among the nine islands of Mundaú.
Praia do Francês
A short drive south, this famed beach pairs a reef-protected turquoise swimming end with a surf-pounded stretch backed by cliffs and seafood shacks.
Mirante da Sereia
The 'Mermaid Lookout' above Garça Torta delivers Maceió's best coastal panorama, where emerald reef flats stripe the sea toward the northern beaches.
Praia do Gunga
Framed by coconut plantations where the Roteiro Lagoon meets the sea, this celebrated day-trip beach is often ranked among Brazil's most beautiful.
Marechal Deodoro Historic Town
Alagoas' colonial former capital, birthplace of Brazil's first president, preserves the gilded São Francisco convent complex above the Manguaba Lagoon.
Catedral Metropolitana de Maceió
The neoclassical 1859 cathedral of Our Lady of Pleasures presides over Praça Dom Pedro II, the dignified heart of Maceió's historic center.
Museu Théo Brandão
In a seafront powder-blue mansion, this folklore museum celebrates Alagoan popular culture, from guerreiro festival costumes to ceramics and cordel literature.
Palácio Floriano Peixoto and Praça dos Martírios
The salmon-pink 1902 governor's palace and its palm-studded plaza, framed by the tiled Igreja Bom Jesus dos Martírios, showcase Maceió's belle-époque core.

train.note: No intercity passenger rail. Maceió has a short CBTU commuter line inland toward Rio Largo, but nothing long-distance. Travel between cities is by coach or plane.

bus.note: No international coaches. The Rodoviária north of the centre has Real Alagoas and Progresso services to Recife (about 4 hours), Aracaju (5) and Salvador (10), plus frequent regional buses down the coast to Barra de São Miguel and Praia do Francês; book through ClickBus (https://www.clickbus.com.br/).

ferry.note: There is no scheduled passenger ferry from Maceió. Jangada sailing rafts take visitors out to the natural pools on the reef at Pajuçara, and catamarans run to the pools at Pontal do Peba - both are excursions rather than transport.

half.name: Barra de São Miguel
half.blurb: A beach town about 30 kilometers south of Maceió where the Sergipe River meets the ocean, with calm lagoon pools and a colonial fort ruin.

full.name: São Miguel dos Milagres
full.blurb: A quiet coastal stretch roughly 100 kilometers north of Maceió known as the Alagoas Maldives, with palm-lined beaches and shallow reef pools.

full.name: Japaratinga
full.blurb: A fishing village on the Alagoas coast north of Maceió with tide pools formed by offshore reefs at low tide.
